phonemes.desc: Short omicron with smooth breathing — the name begins low and unforced.
Delta and short upsilon with sigma [dys] — the compact middle the poets linked to ὀδύσσομαι, 'to hate'.
Sigma plus the diphthong ευ under acute pitch [seús] — the rising, long final syllable of the agentive -εύς names.

pronunciation.approximation: 'oh-dyss-SEWS' — three quick syllables gathering into a long, high final surge, like a wave cresting at the name's end.

kin.label: Greek verb
kin.form: ὀδύσσομαι, 'to be wroth with, to hate' — the Odyssey's own etymology: his grandfather Autolykos names him 'the hated one' (Od. 19.407)

kin.label: Homeric epithets
kin.form: πολύτροπος 'of many turns', πολύμητις 'of many counsels', πολύτλας 'much-enduring'

kin.label: Western Greek
kin.form: dialectal forms with -l- (Ὀλυσσεύς) stand behind the Latin name

pronunciation.note: Odysseús is Tier 1 because the Greek Ὀδυσσεύς contains both stress (the acute on the final syllable) and length (the diphthong ευ). The restoration keeps the acute on ú; the diphthong itself survives in the standard transliteration eu. English 'Odysseus' flattens the pitch that Greek put on the name's last syllable.

domains.title: The Man of Many Turns
domains.subtitle: Cunning, Endurance, and the Long Road Home
domains.lead: Odysseús is the Greeks' fullest study of intelligence under pressure: the strategist of Troy, the wanderer of ten years, the beggar who comes home to a house full of enemies and wins it back with patience, a bow, and a rooted bed. Homer gives him more words than any other hero — his weapon is speech itself.

cards.name: The Strategist
cards.desc: Deviser of the Wooden Horse, and of the name Outis — 'Nobody' — by which he outwitted the Cyclops Polyphêmos.

cards.name: The Wayfarer
cards.desc: Ten years from Troy to Ithaka: Cyclops, Kirke, the dead, the Sirens, Skylla and Charybdis, Kalypso — the sea's whole syllabus.

cards.name: The Returned King
cards.desc: Disguised as a beggar in his own hall, he strings the great bow and takes back house, wife, and kingdom from the suitors.

cards.name: Athena's Favourite
cards.desc: The goddess of counsel delights in him precisely because he is like her: 'among all men you are the best in counsel and speech' (Od. 13).

symbols.name: The great bow
symbols.meaning: The weapon only he could string; the test by which the beggar becomes the king

symbols.name: The olive-trunk bed
symbols.meaning: Built into a living, rooted tree — the immovable sign by which Penelope knows her husband

symbols.name: The scar
symbols.meaning: The boar's-tusk wound from Parnassos, by which the old nurse Eurykleia knows him first

symbols.name: The oar
symbols.meaning: Carried inland until a wayfarer mistakes it for a winnowing-fan — the prophecy of his peace

symbols.name: The ship
symbols.meaning: The vessel of the much-turned man; he loses every one and still comes home

mythology.lead: The Odyssey is his biography, but his story begins in the Iliad and ends in prophecy: war at Troy, ten years of wandering, and a homecoming the gods themselves had to negotiate. He is the one hero of the cycle whose full arc — force, craft, loss, return — the tradition preserves entire.

myths.title: The Wooden Horse
myths.text: When ten years of force had not taken Troy, Odysseús took it in a night by craft. The horse was built by Epeios with Athena's help (Od. 8.492) and carried the flower of the Achaeans within the walls as a pretended offering to appease the very goddess the city had outraged. Odysseús steered the plan through its two greatest dangers: Helen walking the horse's flank and speaking with the voices of the men's wives (Od. 4.274–279), and the priest Laocoön hurling his spear into the wooden side, which rang hollow — a scene the Roman tradition expands into full tragedy (Virgil, Aeneid 2). At midnight the horse opened, the gates received the returning army, and Troy burned. The Odyssey's singers treat the ruse as Odysseús's crowning glory (Od. 8.520), while the heirs of the fallen remembered the same night as the crime that founded their own counter-epic. The myth's unease is its point: Greek heroism could conquer what Greek force could not — but only by teaching the world to fear intelligence as much as courage.

myths.title: Nobody in the Cyclops' Cave
myths.text: In Odyssey 9 the wanderer comes to the island of the Cyclopes and enters the cave of Polyphêmos with twelve of his men. The giant blocks the entrance with a great stone and devours two sailors at each meal; force is impossible, so Odysseús's answer is a name. He tells the Cyclops he is called Outis — 'Nobody' (Od. 9.366) — and then hands him the potent wine of Maron. Drunk and blinded by the fire-hardened olive-stake, the giant bellows that Nobody is killing him, and his neighbors take the joke for silence and walk away. The crew escapes clinging beneath the bellies of the rams, and as the ship pulls off Odysseús cannot resist shouting his true name across the water — winning Poseidôn's wrath and the ten years that followed (Od. 9.526–536). The episode is the poem's deepest meditation on identity: Odysseús survives by annihilating his name, and is nearly destroyed by reclaiming it. The self, Homer suggests, is the one treasure that cannot be shouted home.

myths.title: Kirke's Island and the Road to the Dead
myths.text: On Aiaia, Kirke turns the scouting party into swine — 'their mind remained firm as before' (Od. 10.239–240) — until Odysseús, armed by Hermês with the moly herb, forces her to swear the oath that ends her hostility (Od. 10.343–346). A year of feasting follows, and then the strangest gift in the poem: she sends him where no living sailor has gone, down to the house of Hades to drink blood with the blind seer Teiresias (Od. 10.487–540; 11). There he meets the ghost of his mother, Achilles among the dead, and watches Tityos, Tantalos, and Sisyphos at their eternal labors. The enchantress becomes the hero's teacher, and her island the hinge of the whole epic: before Kirke, Odysseús is a raider fleeing disasters; after her, he is a man who has consulted the dead and knows what his homecoming will cost. The poem's most dangerous woman is also the one who gives it its moral map — a reversal Homer performs without comment, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

myths.title: Kalypso and the Land of the Phaiakians
myths.text: For seven years the nymph Kalypso holds Odysseús on Ogygia, offering him immortality and agelessness — and each day he refuses, choosing Ithaka, its smoke, and a mortal wife (Od. 5.209–224; 7.256–258). Zeús orders his release; Poseidôn wrecks the raft within sight of land (Od. 5.282–381); the naked castaway, kept afloat by Ino-Leukothea's veil, crawls under twin olive bushes and buries himself in leaves 'like a brand under black ash' (Od. 5.483–490). Then comes the strangest rescue in Greek epic: Nausikáa, a princess doing the palace laundry, finds him salt-crusted and terrible — and, because Athena has steadied her heart, brings the stranger home. The Phaiakians feast him, hear his whole tale, and set him on a ship that carries him sleeping to Ithaka (Od. 13). The sequence is the Odyssey's theology in miniature: a man can lose everything except the direction of home, and the gods help only those still crawling toward it.

myths.title: The Bow and the Rooted Bed
myths.text: Twenty years gone, Odysseús enters his own hall disguised as a beggar and endures blows he could repay with blood, because revenge mistimed is ruin (Od. 17–20). Pēnelópē, at the end of her patience, sets the contest: whoever strings the great bow and sends an arrow through twelve axes shall have her (Od. 19.570–587; 21). The suitors fail one by one; the beggar strings it in a motion smooth as a lyre-player's tuning, and the hall runs red (Od. 22). Even then Pēnelópē does not trust her eyes: she orders the bridal bed moved, and Odysseús cries out that it cannot be — he built it himself around a living olive stump, rooted in the earth, the wood planed and inlaid (Od. 23.153–202). Recognition comes not from the face but from the bed. The epic ends by answering its own question: what survives twenty years of wandering is not strength but the rooted thing a man refuses to move. Teiresias's oar still waits — a last journey inland, and a gentle death from the sea (Od. 11.121–137).

lore.syncretism: The western Greeks pronounced his name with -l-, and through them it reached Italy: Latin Ulixēs, English Ulysses. Rome admired his cunning and distrusted it; Virgil's Aeneid makes him the face of Greek deceit, while the philosophers reclaimed him as the Stoic sage. Dante's Ulisse sails beyond the Pillars of Herakles and drowns for the love of knowledge — the Christian epic's answer to Homer. Long before all this, the Odyssey itself had performed the boldest syncretism: it turned a folktale wanderer into the type of every human journey, so that his name, as the common noun 'odyssey', no longer needs him at all.
lore.culturalLegacy: He is the most rewritten figure of the ancient world: Sophocles' divided portraits, Euripides' stage villain, Tennyson's aging voyager ('to strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield'), Joyce's Ulysses, in which a Dublin advertisement canvasser lives the whole epic in a day, Kazantzakis's modern sequel, Cavafy's Ithaka — 'wise as you will have become, so full of experience' — and a hundred films and novels. Space probes and wanderers' memoirs borrow the noun he became. Restoring Odysseús keeps the stress Greek put on his last syllable: the name itself rises at the end, like a mast coming over the horizon.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every other hero of the Trojan cycle is defined by what he can overpower; Odysseús is defined by what he can outlast. The epic tests him with each kind of loss — companions, ships, time, fame, even identity: he survives the Cyclops precisely by becoming Nobody, and he survives Kalypso precisely by refusing to become a god. Between those two refusals lies his whole philosophy. A man is not his name, and yet the name is all that comes home.

The ending refuses triumph. The suitors are dead, the hall is his, and still the wife he won must test him, and the test is not valor but knowledge: only the true husband knows the bed cannot move because it was built on a living root. That rootedness is the answer to all the wandering — the one unmoving thing in a life of motion, grown not made. And beyond even that, Teiresias's oar waits: the promise that he must carry the sea inland until it is no longer recognized. The man of many turns earns his peace only where nobody knows what an oar is — where even his story cannot follow him.
lore.archaeology: Ithaki, the island that still bears his name, has Mycenaean remains at Pelikata and Aetos, and at Polis Bay a cave sanctuary of the Nymphs whose votive deposits run from the Late Bronze Age to the Roman period — the very cave where later Ithacans placed Odysseús's homecoming, and where a Hellenistic terracotta fragment inscribed ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥΣΣΕΙ, 'a prayer to Odysseus', attests his hero-cult. The Bronze Age site above Polis Bay, long called the School of Homer, remains conjectural as his palace. Beyond Ithaka his cult is epigraphic and scattered; his truest monument is Homer's text.
